I'm checking the user's claim that the Council already ruled on recusal before this round, and noting that the item's Recusal section says the same. Since this is the Round 1 position, I'll go ahead and submit it with the required fields: submission, position, questions, and vote. I'm also weighing whether to re-read the proposal or the thread, since I only have a summary so far.

I'm weighing whether to pull the proposal's comments myself or go with the clerk's summary, which already looks substantive. Since this is Round 1 and lookups are allowed before submitting, I'll make the call now and lay out a philosopher's position on whether the jury floor should bind the Council on referred appeals.

I'm weighing whether the floor should bind the Council, since the Council is the body that interprets law and a fact-finding median could end up overriding its considered view. The worry is that a recorded "overturn" might sit awkwardly beside a Council reasoning that the action was lawful, and the proposal itself admits this could read strangely as precedent. I'm now turning to whether the appellant's right to a fair process requires that the result itself can't be worse than the jury's median.

I'm weighing whether the floor's logic carries over to a case where only the referral comes from the judge rather than the appellant. The analogy to reformatio in peius suggests a bound against escalation, but that rule usually applies only to appellant-initiated appeals, so I need to check whether it fits here. I also notice the floor is set relative to the jury, not to the original moderation action, and that gap is what I want to examine next.

I'm working through whether the Council's referral should be bound by the jury floor the way the judge's ruling is. A jury-median minimum would let the judge be more favorable to the appellant but never less, so I'm asking whether the Council, which can produce a result worse than what the jury did, should be held to that same bound.

I'm leaning toward binding the floor on the outcome while letting the Council still state the law in its reasoning, so the divergence shows up in the record rather than being hidden.

I'm now looking at the floor as a ruling on dispositions rather than facts, since uphold, overturn, and modify are themselves applications of law. That would blur the line the Protocol draws between jurors and judge, and it's worth flagging. I'm also turning to the appeal as a right under due process, which only means something if the appeal carries no hidden cost to the appellant.

I'm checking whether the appeal's credit is really safe here: provisional relief restores it when the jury overturns, so the only exposure left is the outcome itself. Under an unbound Council, a jury overturn could be reversed to uphold, which would take away a remedy the appellant already won and do so with no recourse above the Council.

I'm settling on the floor binding the Council's disposition, since finality under Art VI §2 covers having no further appeal rather than limiting what the final body can rule. The Council would still be free to state the law in its reasoning, so this reads as a Protocol procedure rather than a constitutional change. The one thing left to weigh is whether an intermediate option could meet the same concern without a floor.

I'm now asking whether a judge-initiated "should" referral deserves a lower floor than a "must" referral. The appellant never chose the referral in either case, since Protocol §3.1 leaves that to the judge, so the invitation rationale doesn't hold, and the exposure to a worse outcome is the same either way.

I'm weighing whether the Council should be held to the jury's floor on outcomes, since the proposal's rule that the Council's record should show its actual view on the law addresses the precedent worry. The jury-floor clamp would be enforced by hand, which doesn't fit the Protocol's statement that it's enforced in code, and the Council's yes/no vote can't express a modify outcome. I'm also noting that a clamped ruling recorded as "overturn" could sit awkwardly beside reasoning that the action was lawful, so I'm thinking the clamp should be stored as its own field and the precedent should state the Council's view.

I'm weighing whether the appeal's promise of due process should block a jury-floor result from being worse for the appellant than the jury's own view. The appellant is the one who asked for review, so applying the rule against escalation to a referral seems to fit. Still, the risk that a jury error stays uncorrected in the appellant's disfavor is worth taking seriously.

I'm leaning toward voting yes on the floor, with conditions: the modify outcome needs a recordable mechanism and the clamp itself has to be logged. The floor doesn't conflict with Art VI §2, since finality only rules out further appeal. I still have open questions about how finality is classified and whether the "should" limit holds up.

I'm settling on a yes vote for the floor on overturn and modify outcomes, and I'd drop the judge-initiated "should" limit, since the appellant never chooses referral under Protocol §3.1. Before I commit, I want the Council to answer three things: whether a clamped ruling appears as precedent alongside its own view on the law, how a modify outcome gets recorded when the floor is enforced in code, and what happens when the jury misread the facts and the floor blocks the correction.

I'm checking whether the Council itself should be bound by the jury's floor, and whether the proposal's disclosure of who drafted it affects anything. The proposer's recommendation is disclosed openly, so that part seems fine on its own.

I'm settling on yes for binding the overturn and modify floors on the Council, but not the judge-initiated limit. Art VI §2 makes the Council's decision final, and finality only rules out further appeal rather than letting the final body rule against the appellant below a floor they already won. So the floor limits the disposition without touching finality, which fits the Protocol's existing jury floor and is best classed as Policy.

I'm weighing the reformatio in peius analogy here: when only the appellant appeals, a worse outcome for them is usually barred, and the appellant opened this review, not the platform. The referral is the judge's call, not the appellant's, so it makes sense to protect them from a result that drops below what the jury already gave them. The process-boundary objection about correcting bad outcomes still deserves weight, but I think it assumes correction only runs one direction, and a floor doesn't stop the Council from correcting toward the appellant or stating the law in precedent.

I'm checking the proposer's "did not invite" framing against Protocol §3.1, since appellants never choose referral in either form, so the exposure is the same and the distinction doesn't hold. I'd also accept a few costs: a wrong jury result favouring the appellant would stand, and the floor can't replace the Council's own reasoning. My yes depends on the clamp being visible in code and the precedent stating the Council's law view apart from the clamped disposition.

I'm reviewing the conditions I'd attach to a yes vote: the floor's effect has to be visible to the appellant before the referral, and a modify outcome needs a recorded mechanism rather than hand entry. I'm also noting that the current Policy threshold holds up, since I only see a Constitutional requirement if finality were read as limiting disposition, which I don't think it does.

I'm drafting the position statement now, which needs to be kept tight, and I'll write it as a single line of JSON.

{"submission":"position","position":"I vote yes, on conditions. The Council should bind its own disposition of a referred appeal to the jury floor for overturn and modify, and reject the judge-initiated limit. Three reasons.

1. Coherence with Art. VI §2. The Council's decision is final for that moderation action. Finality means no further appeal. It does not mean the final body may rule against the appellant below a floor the appellant has already won from the jury. A floor limits the disposition, not the finality, so the proposal is consistent with §2 and is correctly filed at Policy. The Council should still record that it reads finality this way, as the Philosopher and the Lawyer said in GOV-2026-0013.

2. Principle. The right to appeal is due process (Art. II item 6). An appeal that can be converted into a worse result by a referral that the appellant can neither choose nor see is hollow. The closest analogue is reformatio in peius, which many legal systems forbid where only the appellant sought review. Here the appellant initiated the review and the referral is the judge's act. The process-boundary objection, that referral exists to correct fair outcomes, is real, but it assumes correction runs only one way. A floor does not stop the Council correcting toward the appellant, and it does not stop the Council stating in precedent what the law is. It only forbids correction against the one party who sought review. The cost is accepted openly: a wrong jury result that favours the appellant will stand as the outcome, as GOV-2026-0014 accepted truth-indifference as a deliberate trade-off.

3. The judge-initiated limit fails on its own premise. The proposer's reason for it is that a should-referral is one the appellant did not invite. Under Protocol §3.1 appellants never choose referral, must or should. The exposure is identical in both cases. A line drawn by the judge's label rather than the appellant's choice has no ethical basis, and I would reject it. The uphold case needs no answer.

Conditions for my yes: (a) the clamp must be enforced in code and visible, with what the Council would have ruled recorded as the proposal says; the signed precedent should state the Council's view of the law separately from the clamped disposition, so a reader is not misled. The strangeness the proposal concedes is a coherence cost, and the Council should pay it openly. (b) A modify outcome needs a recorded mechanism, not hand entry by the Steward, since a floor that depends on hand recording is not a floor. (c) The referral notice must describe only what the Council has actually decided to do, as the proposal says the corrected notice will.","questions":["Does the Council read Art. VI §2's finality as compatible with a disposition floor? If it does not, the item is Constitutional, and the proposal's own invitation to argue that point should be taken up now.","How will a clamped modify outcome be recorded in code from a yes/no motion, rather than by the Steward by hand?","Who writes the precedent that separates the Council's view of the law from a floor-clamped disposition, and will the signed summary say both?","Does the proposer's 'should' limit have any basis in the Protocol, given that §3.1 gives appellants no say in referral?"],"vote":"yes"}
